examples: Here is your food. Enjoy your meal.
I made this. Enjoy your meal.
Enjoy your meal. I will go first.
nuance: A warm phrase you say to other people before they eat, not about yourself. Servers and hosts use it constantly in everyday Korean dining situations.
mistakes: Do not say it about your own meal.

english: I look forward to working with you
usage: Please take good care of it
I look forward to working with you
Please treat me well going forward
examples: I start working today. I look forward to it.
Please take care of the documents.
Please take good care of my child.
nuance: A polite set phrase used when asking someone to take care of something or when starting a new relationship. It builds goodwill and has no exact one-word English match.
mistakes: It is not literally a request for help.

examples: The floor is slippery. Be careful.
Be careful on the night road.
nuance: A caring polite phrase used both as a real safety warning and as a friendly farewell. Koreans often add a noun in front to specify what to watch out for.
mistakes: Drop the polite ending only with close friends.

examples: I am not sure either. I will check again.
I do not know this words meaning.
I do not know when it will end.
nuance: The natural everyday way to say you do not know something. The 겠 part softens it, making it sound more humble and polite than the blunt form 몰라요.
mistakes: 몰라요 can sound a bit curt.

examples: Hold on, let me take this call.
Just a sec, I am coming.
nuance: A very common short phrase to ask someone to wait briefly or to politely get past them. It is friendly and casual yet still polite enough for strangers.
mistakes: Use 잠시만요 in very formal settings.

examples: Thanks for helping. You are welcome.
You are welcome, it was nothing.
nuance: A polite reply to thank you, similar to you are welcome. It sounds a little formal, so close friends often use lighter replies like 응 or 별말씀을 instead.
mistakes: Younger people may find it slightly stiff.

usage: Not at all, I gladly did it
examples: It went well thanks to you. Dont mention it.
You are so kind. Dont mention it.
Not at all, of course I should help.
nuance: A humble polite reply used to brush off thanks or compliments, much like dont mention it. It signals modesty and is common among adults in courteous everyday conversation.
mistakes: It also deflects praise, not just thanks.

examples: Did you enjoy it? Come again.
nuance: A warm farewell that shop and restaurant staff say to invite customers back. As a customer you usually just reply 네, 감사합니다 rather than repeating it.
mistakes: Staff say it, customers rarely do.

examples: Here is the coffee you ordered.
nuance: Used when physically handing something to someone, like here you go. Note that 여기요 alone is the common way to call a server, so context decides the meaning.
mistakes: 여기요 alone means excuse me, server.

usage: How much time does it take?
nuance: A key travel phrase for asking how much time something needs. Add a method like 버스로 or a place with 까지 in front to make your question more specific.

examples: What is this? I have never seen it.
What is this? Is it spicy?
nuance: The most basic everyday way to ask what an object is while pointing at it. 이거 is the casual spoken form of 이것, so it sounds natural and friendly.
mistakes: For people use 누구예요 not 뭐예요.

usage: I will pop to the restroom
examples: I will use the restroom. Back soon.
Excuse me, may I use the restroom?
밥 먹기 전에 화장실 좀 쓸게요.
I will use the restroom before eating.
nuance: A polite casual way to announce you are stepping away to the restroom. The word 좀 softens it, and 쓸게요 signals your own intention rather than asking permission.
mistakes: Add 써도 돼요 when permission is needed.
